procedural_history.originating_court: Special Judge, Kangra, Dharamshala, Himachal Pradesh
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 25.04.2014 of the High Court of Himachal Pradesh at Shimla in Cr. MMO. No. 6 of 2014, dismissing petitions under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Cr.P.C.) for quashing of FIRs.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants filed petitions under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Cr.P.C.) before the High Court of Himachal Pradesh for quashing of two FIRs (FIR No. 12 of 2013 and FIR No. 14 of 2013). The High Court dismissed these petitions vide common judgment dated April 25, 2014.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants filed Special Leave Petitions (SLPs) against the High Court's judgment, which were converted into Criminal Appeals Nos. 1258-1259 of 2018. The Supreme Court issued notice on January 5, 2015, and granted a stay of further proceedings in the case arising out of the said FIRs pending before the Special Judge. The stay was extended from time to time and was continuing.

decision.appeal_result: Disposing of the appeals and the writ petition

issue.issue_text: Whether the appeals have become infructuous.

facts: Respondent No. 2 argued that the appeals had become infructuous because a chargesheet had since been filed in the case.
The appellants countered that the chargesheet was filed and cognizance was taken while their appeals were already pending before the Supreme Court.
The appellants also filed a new writ petition to challenge the subsequent chargesheet and cognizance order.
The State (Respondent No. 1) informed the Court that it had decided not to continue with the criminal proceedings and supported the appellants' case.
law: The Supreme Court has inherent power under Articles 136 and 142 of the Constitution to quash an FIR, chargesheet, or other criminal proceedings at any stage in order to do complete justice in a matter pending before it.
application: The Court noted that the events which supposedly rendered the appeal infructuous (the filing of the chargesheet) occurred during the pendency of the proceedings before it.
The Court accepted the appellants' argument that it had the power to quash proceedings at any stage, including after a chargesheet has been filed, to ensure complete justice.
Furthermore, the Court considered the State's decision not to prosecute the case, which supported the idea that continuing the proceedings served no purpose.
reasoning.conclusion: In view of its discussion and the fact that it has the power to quash proceedings at any stage to do complete justice, the Supreme Court rejected the argument of Respondent No. 2 that the appeals had become infructuous.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court has the inherent power under Articles 32, 136, and 142 of the Constitution to quash an FIR, chargesheet, and cognizance order to do complete justice.

facts: The appellants filed a Writ Petition (Criminal) No. 135 of 2017 in the Supreme Court to quash a chargesheet and a cognizance order.
This writ petition was filed while appeals (Special Leave Petitions) against the High Court's refusal to quash the initial FIR were already pending before the Supreme Court.
An argument was made that a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution was not maintainable to challenge a cognizance order.
law: The Supreme Court has inherent power under Articles 32, 136, and 142 of the Constitution to quash an FIR, chargesheet, and other criminal proceedings to do complete justice in a matter pending before it.

Precedents such as *Delhi Judicial Service Association, Tis Hazari Court, Delhi v. State of Gujarat & Ors.* and *Monica Kumar & Anr. v. State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.* establish that there is no restriction on this power of the Court.
application: The Court acknowledged the argument that a writ petition under Article 32 might not be maintainable against a cognizance order.
However, the Court decided to entertain the writ petition due to the "peculiar facts" of the case.
The key fact was that the matter was already pending before the Supreme Court through the Special Leave Petitions challenging the High Court's refusal to quash the FIR.
Given the pendency of these related proceedings, the Court found it appropriate to also consider the challenge to the subsequent chargesheet and cognizance order to do complete justice.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted that it has the inherent power under Articles 32, 136, and 142 to quash an FIR, chargesheet, and cognizance order to do complete justice. It exercised this power by entertaining the writ petition, reasoning that the unique circumstance of related appeals already being pending before it justified such an intervention.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in refusing to exercise its powers under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. to quash the criminal proceedings.

facts: The High Court had refused to quash criminal proceedings against the appellants.
The High Court's reasoning was that the power under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. is to be exercised cautiously and in the rarest of cases.
The High Court found that the FIR and the investigation material disclosed a prima facie case for trial.
It also dismissed the appellants' arguments of mala fides, stating that such allegations made after the FIR is lodged are of no consequence.
law: The Supreme Court reiterated the principles governing the exercise of inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 Cr.P.C.
This power is an exception, not the rule, and must be used carefully and with caution.
It is justified when its exercise prevents a grave miscarriage of justice, such as when an accused would be unnecessarily harassed by a trial that is likely to end in acquittal.
The purpose of this power is to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or to otherwise secure the ends of justice.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court conducted a "shallow examination" of the case and "glossed over the material facts."
It held that the High Court failed to recognize that the pertinent facts were sufficient to demonstrate that no criminal case was actually made out.

Specifically, the Supreme Court noted that the High Court overlooked a crucial fact: all the concerned officers who had made the decision at the heart of the case had already been let off on the ground that they had committed no wrong.

The Supreme Court criticized the High Court for only noting the cautionary principles of Section 482 without applying them to the specific circumstances, which warranted the exercise of this power to do substantial justice.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in refusing to exercise its powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. It found that the High Court failed to properly examine the facts, which clearly showed that allowing the proceedings to continue would be an abuse of process and a miscarriage of justice. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment and quashed the criminal proceedings.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appeals have become infructuous.
appellant_arguments: The appellant implicitly argued that the appeals were not infructuous, contending that the proceedings should be quashed even after the chargesheet was filed.
respondent_arguments: Respondent No. 2 argued that the appeals had become infructuous, likely because the investigation was completed and chargesheets were filed during the pendency of the proceedings.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court has the inherent power under Articles 32, 136, and 142 of the Constitution to quash an FIR, chargesheet, and cognizance order to do complete justice.
appellant_arguments: The appellants implicitly argued for the court to exercise its inherent power by filing the appeals and writ petition to quash all proceedings against them.
respondent_arguments: Respondent No. 2 argued that the only procedure prescribed in law for withdrawal was under Section 321 of the Cr.P.C., which was not followed.
Respondent No. 2 argued that there were serious allegations against the accused persons and no case for quashing the chargesheet was made out.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in refusing to exercise its powers under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. to quash the criminal proceedings.
appellant_arguments: The matter was, at best, a civil dispute between the parties.
The dispute was mala fidely given the cloak of a criminal proceeding to harass the appellants.
The High Court erroneously ignored the legal principle 'Actus Reus Non Facit Reum Nisi Mens Sit Rea' (an act does not make a person guilty unless the mind is also guilty).
The case for quashing was covered by the principles laid down in the judgment of State of Haryana & Ors. v. Bhajan Lal & Ors.
respondent_arguments: Respondent No. 2 argued that there were serious allegations against the accused persons.
Respondent No. 2 contended that no case for quashing the chargesheet/challan was made out.

cases.case_name: State of Haryana & Ors. v. Bhajan Lal & Ors.
cases.principle: All courts possess inherent powers to do right and undo wrong in the course of the administration of justice. This inherent jurisdiction, though wide, must be exercised sparingly, carefully, and with caution to do real and substantial justice.

cases.case_name: Vineet Kumar & Ors. v. State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
cases.principle: All courts possess inherent powers to do right and undo wrong in the course of the administration of justice. This inherent jurisdiction, though wide, must be exercised sparingly, carefully, and with caution to do real and substantial justice.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The inherent jurisdiction of the High Court under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. is an exceptional power, not the rule, and must be exercised sparingly, carefully, and with caution. This power is to be invoked only when it is evident that a grave miscarriage of justice would occur if the trial were allowed to proceed, particularly where it would lead to unnecessary harassment of the accused and the trial is prima facie likely to end in an acquittal.
obiter: All courts, whether civil or criminal, possess inherent powers necessary to do right and undo a wrong in the course of the administration of justice, based on the principle 'quando lex aliquid alicui concedit, concedere videtur et id sine quo res ipsae esse non potest' (when the law gives a person anything it gives him that without which it cannot exist).
The exercise of inherent jurisdiction is ex debito justitiae (as a matter of right) to do real and substantial justice.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Upon a 360° scanning of the matter, the Court concluded that the essential elements of criminal intent or criminal acts were lacking. The dispute was, at best, civil in nature, and ex facie, no case of cheating, fraud, or criminal breach of trust was made out against the appellants. Consequently, allowing the criminal proceedings to continue would serve no purpose and would constitute an abuse of the court's process, particularly as the State (Respondent No. 1) had indicated it did not wish to prosecute.
legal_tests_applied: The test for exercising inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 Cr.P.C., which is to be used 'sparingly, carefully and with caution' and only when its exercise is justified to prevent abuse of the process of court or to secure the ends of justice. This power is an exception to be applied when 'grave miscarriage of justice would be committed if the trial is allowed to proceed where the accused would be harassed unnecessarily' and when 'prima facie it appears to the Court that the trial could likely to be ended in acquittal.'

The principle that a chargesheet and a cognizance order are not final judicial orders but are a 'preliminary process in criminal law and is open to challenge in higher judicial fora such as this Court.' This justifies the court's intervention even after these stages have been completed.

The legal maxim 'Actus Reus Non Facit Reum Nisi Mens Sit Rea' (an act does not make a person guilty unless the mind is also guilty), which the High Court was found to have erroneously ignored, and which the Supreme Court applied by finding that 'the elements of criminal intent or criminal acts are lacking.'
policy_considerations: The inherent power of all courts exists 'to do the right and to undo a wrong in course of administration of justice on the principle quando lex aliquid alicui concedit, concedere videtur et id sine quo res ipsae esse non potest (when the law gives a person anything it gives him that without which it cannot exist).'
The authority of the court exists for the 'advancement of justice and if any attempt is made to abuse that authority so as to produce injustice the Court has power to prevent abuse.'
The court's power should not 'be inhibited when the circumstances warrant exercise of such a power to do substantial justice to the parties.'
It is futile to continue proceedings when the state itself does not wish to prosecute, as 'no purpose would be served in continuing with these proceedings.'
